Electric charge

 Home Physics Branches of physics Electromagnetism
OurBigBook.com Words: 15k Articles: 170
Electric charge is an additive, signed property of matter that determines its coupling to the electromagnetic field. Write a particle's electric charge as q, or a collection's total electric charge as Q; the SI unit is the coulomb, C. A stationary test particle in an electric field experiences electric force F=qE, while motion adds the magnetic part of the Lorentz force. Electric charge both produces an electric field and determines the response to one. For two stationary point particles in vacuum, Coulomb's law makes like signs repel and opposite signs attract. The choice of which sign to call positive is a convention, used consistently: protons carry +e and electrons carry −e, where e is the elementary charge. [ref].
Additivity means adding signed electric charges, rather than their magnitudes:
Q=∑i​qi​,Q=e(Np​−Ne​)
(1)
for ordinary matter containing Np​ protons, Ne​ electrons, and electrically neutral neutrons. A toy collection with seven protons and ten electrons has Q=−3e, however much neutral material accompanies it. Charge neutrality means Q=0; it does not mean an absence of charged constituents. Nor does it guarantee an absence of electric force: the spatial arrangement of positive and negative electric charges matters, as illustrated by an electric dipole. This makes a tiny imbalance in an otherwise nearly neutral object physically important. [ref].
Charge conservation states that a collection closed to transport of electric charge keeps its total signed Q. If n electrons move from object A to object B without other exchange, then ΔQA​=+ne and ΔQB​=−ne; the sum is unchanged. The amount of positive electric charge alone need not be conserved: creation of an electron and a Positron adds opposite electric charges with zero sum. These bookkeeping rules let us distinguish separation or transport of electric charge from creation of net electric charge. [ref].
A simple motivating experiment uses two charge-producing paddles, a conducting pail on an insulating support, a grounded outer shield and a high-input-impedance electrometer. Zero the pail, then isolate it. Rub the initially neutral paddles together, keeping their charged surfaces away from other objects. Lower each deeply into the pail without touching: the electrometer gives opposite signs. Inserting both together tests cancellation. For a separate contact test, insert one charged paddle without touching and withdraw it: the reading returns to zero. Repeat after zeroing, this time touching the inner wall before withdrawal: a residual reading shows transfer of electric charge. Zero the pail and reinsert the paddle to test how much electric charge remains on it. PASCO describes these procedures in Basic Electrostatics System manual, demonstrations 1A and 1B, printed pp. 13–16.
The crucial control is withdrawal without contact: a response during insertion can come from electrostatic induction, which redistributes the pail's existing electric charge. In the fixed-geometry approximation, the electrometer measures electric potential difference proportional to enclosed electric charge, with conversion set by effective capacitance; a voltage reading is not already a measurement in coulombs. Opposite readings and their cancellation test additivity and charge conservation within resolution. Leakage or accidental contact spoils that interpretation, and contact need not transfer all the paddle's electric charge. This macroscopic experiment cannot resolve elementary charge steps: that requires the much smaller particles of the oil drop experiment.

Surface charge (QS​=∫S​σdS)

Words: 25
Electric charge OurBigBook.com
Electric charge concentrated on a surface. Its local amount per unit area is the surface charge density σ; in vacuum the jump of the outward normal electric field is σ/ϵ0​ by Gauss's law.

Charge distribution

Words: 17
Electric charge OurBigBook.com
The spatial arrangement of electric charge, described by a charge density, a surface charge density, a linear charge density, or discrete point charges as appropriate.

Electron repulsion

Words: 33
Electric charge OurBigBook.com
Electron repulsion is the repulsive electrostatic interaction between electrons. In a metal complex it affects pairing costs and many-electron transition energies, so a measured absorption maximum is not always identical to a one-electron orbital splitting.

Free charge

Words: 48
Electric charge OurBigBook.com
In macroscopic electromagnetism, free charge is the part of the charge density represented explicitly as ρf​, separately from bound charge associated with the electric polarization of matter. The electric displacement field satisfies ∇⋅D=ρf​. The word free does not imply zero force or zero energy: it distinguishes this source from the polarization response in the chosen material description.

Charge invariance

Words: 63
Electric charge OurBigBook.com
Charge invariance means that the total electric charge of a specified collection of particles is unchanged by a Lorentz transformation. It differs from conservation of electric charge, which compares the same isolated system at different times. For a convective charge distribution with rest density ρ0​, the four-current is Jμ=ρ0​Uμ, where Uμ is its four-velocity; its measured charge density increases under a boost while the simultaneous spatial volume contracts, leaving total charge unchanged.

Space charge

Words: 13
Electric charge OurBigBook.com
Electric charge distributed through a region, whose own electric field can alter the motion of further charged particles.

Elementary charge (e=1.602176634×10−19C)

Words: 2k Articles: 3
Electric charge OurBigBook.com
The elementary charge is the positive magnitude e of the electron's electric charge, not the signed electric charge of the electron itself:
qelectron​=−e,qproton​=+e,e=1.602176634×10−19Cexactly in SI.
(2)
Since the 2019 revision of the SI, this numerical value defines the ampere together with the definition of the second; 1C=1As. Thus today's numerical exactness is a choice of units, whereas measured electric charges still have experimental uncertainty. An oil drop experiment can test charge quantization and the apparatus calibration; it does not supply a new uncertain defining value of e in today's SI. [ref].
For ordinary isolated chemical atoms, ions and charged objects whose net electric charge is counted through protons and electrons, charge quantization gives Q=ne with signed integer n. A neutral chemical atom that loses two electrons becomes an ion of electric charge +2e. A toy object with 109 excess electrons has Q=−0.1602176634nC. Conversely, the scale 1nC/e≃6.24×109 explains why laboratory electric charge often looks continuous: billions of microscopic increments fit into a small macroscopic amount. Averaged charge density is a continuum description, not a claim that each particle has an arbitrarily divisible electric charge.
The ordinary-matter qualifier matters. In the Standard Model, quarks have electric charges +2e/3 or −e/3, and antiquarks have the opposite signs. Confinement means these are constituents of hadrons, not isolated fractionally charged particles collected by an oil drop experiment. The usual valence quark sums give 2(2e/3)−e/3=e for a proton and 2e/3−2(e/3)=0 for a neutron. Thus elementary charge should not be defined as the smallest nonzero electric charge of every constituent in particle theory. [ref].
The beautiful experimental idea behind the oil drop experiment is to determine a microscopic electric charge by watching a visible carrier move. In his 1913 paper, Millikan timed the descent and electrically driven ascent of individual oil drops, repeatedly changing a drop's electric charge through capture of air ions. His apparatus used parallel plates separated by 16mm, a roughly 5300V source, and an optical scale to measure travel distances. He reported multiple relationships among a given drop's inferred electric charges. He also found that uncorrected Stokes's law gave a size-dependent inferred elementary unit, and introduced a pressure-dependent slip correction. These were measured relationships with calibration and model uncertainties, not exact readings of today's defined e. [ref].
A modern instructional implementation sprays low-volatility oil of known density through a plate aperture, illuminates the drops, and follows one through a calibrated optical scale. Measure the plate spacing d, electric potential difference V, air temperature and pressure. Time a fixed distance L with the electric field off to get a terminal falling speed vf​=L/tf​. Then choose the field polarity to drive the same drop upward and measure vr​=L/tr​. Repeat timings at a fixed electric charge, and compare before and after an ion-capture event. The same drop is especially useful because its radius and mass need not be inferred anew for each charge state. [ref].
Here is the leading continuum model, retaining buoyancy. Assume a drop shaped as a sphere of radius a, oil and air densities ρo​ and ρa​, air dynamic viscosity η, and gravitational acceleration g. Define the downward effective weight W and positive linear drag coefficient k by
W=34πa3​(ρo​−ρa​)g,k=6πηa,E≃d∣V∣​.
(3)
At terminal velocity, the net force vanishes. Falling with no electric field, the upward drag force balances weight minus buoyancy. Rising with the electric force upward, the drag force reverses and joins the downward effective weight:
kvf​=W,∣q∣E=W+kvr​=k(vf​+vr​).
(4)
Consequently the uncorrected estimates are
a=2(ρo​−ρa​)g9ηvf​​​,∣q∣=∣V∣6πηa(vf​+vr​)d​.
(5)
The observed direction of response, with known field polarity, supplies the sign of q. A suspended drop gives the alternative balance ∣q∣E=W, but it still requires a determination of W: balancing a drop alone does not determine its electric charge.
For an explicitly invented continuum example, stipulate a=1μm, ρo​=900kgm−3, ρa​=1.2kgm−3, η=1.8×10−5Pas, g=9.81ms−2, q=−5e and a downward E=105Vm−1. The balances predict W≃3.69×10−14N, vf​≃0.109mms−1 and vr​≃0.127mms−1. Substituting those speeds recovers ∣q∣=5e within rounding. This checks the algebra; it is not a precision prediction for real micrometre drops, which need a slip correction.
The inference has two distinct parts. Compare inferred electric charges or charge changes with a common unit, seeking qi​≃ni​e within uncertainty, rather than demanding exact ratios of rounded measurements. Then establish the absolute scale through electric field, density, dynamic viscosity and distance/time calibration. If the observed steps are all even multiples, their common spacing alone cannot exclude an unobserved smaller unit. Air motion, evaporation and mistimed crossings can alter inferred electric charge without an ion-capture event. Small Reynolds number supports Stokes's law, but does not by itself justify its no-slip continuum coefficient: a significant ratio of air mean free path to drop radius requires a slip correction. Millikan's comparison of different drop sizes and pressures addressed that systematic limitation; the modern PASCO manual also includes the correction. Agreement supports charge quantization for the observed carriers within experimental resolution, rather than proving a universal statement about every possible particle.
Multiplying e by the Avogadro constant gives the Faraday constant, F=NA​e, the electric charge per mole of singly charged carriers. This connects counting individual electric charges with bulk electrochemistry. [ref].

Oil drop experiment

Words: 909 Articles: 2
Elementary charge OurBigBook.com
The oil drop experiment infers an oil drop's electric charge from its motion under gravity, buoyancy, drag and a calibrated electric field. Repeated changes of a single drop's electric charge reveal discrete steps; see the model, experimental procedure and limitations in elementary charge.

Oil drop charge readout and calibration

Words: 359
Oil drop experiment OurBigBook.com
Robert Andrews Millikan's 1911 protocol alternated electrically driven ascent with timed descent after short-circuiting the plates; a changed ascent speed signalled ion capture.[ref]
His 1913 refinements checked voltage before and after runs, calibrated optical distance and the clock, compared independent air-dynamic viscosity measurements, and varied pressure to test slip.[ref] His 1924 lecture describes suppressing convection, switching the electric field, neutralizing drops, and reproducing smallest observed electrical speed increments.[ref]
Harvey Fletcher's posthumous account recalls building the first oil apparatus and measuring with Robert Andrews Millikan; priority for suggesting oil remains uncertain.[ref]
To interpret the readout, keep one drop and one electric field polarity. Let ui​ be its signed upward terminal velocity in charge state i, and let vf​>0 be its field-off falling speed. Use the linear drag coefficient k already defined in elementary charge, with any required gas slip correction to Stokes drag included. Provided the drop's radius, surrounding air and electric field remain fixed, its electrical speed increment is
Si​=ui​+vf​,∣qi​∣=Ek​Si​,∣qj​∣∣qi​∣​=Sj​Si​​,Δ∣q∣=Ek​(ui+1​−ui​).
(6)
These relations apply while the electric force points upward in every state. A drop may still descend, with ui​<0, when that force is too weak to support it. A held drop has ui​=0 and therefore Si​=vf​, rather than zero electrical response. A neutral drop has Si​=0: its signed terminal velocity agrees with field-off descent. Thus neither raw upward speed nor the ability to hold a drop is itself a count of electrons.
The ratios cancel a fixed k/E, even if its value is poorly known. This is why relative charge quantization and absolute measurement calibration are different questions. A changed field-off vf​ warns that evaporation, air motion or another change has spoiled comparison of charge states. A stable vf​ is useful evidence but cannot exclude every compensating change. Repeat field-off checks around a proposed jump, allow the terminal velocity under linear drag to settle after switching, and propagate measurement uncertainty in both the field-on and field-off readings. Reusing a single estimate of vf​ gives the different Si​ a shared covariance.

Charge lattice inference from oil drops (qi​≃ni​e)

Words: 517
Oil drop experiment OurBigBook.com
An integer pattern must survive the stated measurement uncertainty. For an original simulated example, choose a reference electric charge Q∗​>0, define yi​=∣qi​∣/Q∗​, and stipulate state means
y=(2.03, 2.96, 5.02, 3.99),σi​=0.08.
(7)
Here each σi​ is an independent standard uncertainty of a state mean, before shared calibration effects. The generator constructs repeated noisy observations with these means; the numbers are deliberately chosen, not historical data. There is no conversion of Q∗​ to coulombs and no measured value of the elementary charge in this example.
For a candidate spacing a>0 in units of Q∗​ and proposed integers ni​, use weighted least squares:
χ2(a,n)=∑i​σi2​(yi​−ni​a)2​,a=∑i​ni2​/σi2​∑i​ni​yi​/σi2​​,u(a)=(∑i​σi2​ni2​​)−1/2.
(8)
The last two expressions follow by differentiating the quadratic in a and propagating the independent errors. They are conditional on fixed, correct integer assignments and the stated error model. They do not include uncertainty from choosing those assignments. For n=(2,3,5,4), they give a=1, u(a)≃0.01089, and χ2=0.46875. Such a small residual is compatible with this chosen error scale; it is not evidence that the errors vanish. A chi-squared distribution interpretation additionally needs the appropriate normal distribution error model and allowance for the fitted parameter; searching many assignments changes that interpretation.
The obstruction is identifiability: replacing (a,ni​) by (a/m,mni​) for any positive integer m leaves every predicted reading unchanged. In particular, an e-spaced pattern also fits an e/2 lattice using even indices. Even the coarsest well-fitting spacing need not be the physical unit: a dataset containing only even charge states can have twice that unit. Worse, if arbitrarily fine spacings and unrestricted integers are allowed, rounding each yi​/a gives
minn​χ2(a,n)≤4a2​∑i​σi2​1​⟶0as a⟶0.
(9)
Consequently a finite fit cannot prove a minimal transferable electric charge. Reproducible smallest observed jumps supply additional evidence; interpreting them as single-carrier transfers requires independent physical support. One visibly abrupt transition could contain several unresolved transfers. In the simulation the successive differences are 0.93, 2.06, and −1.03, each with standard uncertainty 2​(0.08)≃0.1131. These support changes near a,2a,−a conditional on that unit; they equally support 2,4,−2 units of a/2. Neighboring differences share a state reading and are therefore correlated, even though the state means were stipulated independent.
A shared scale error can preserve every apparent integer relation. To first order, an independent fractional scale standard uncertainty s adds s2a2ni​nj​ to the covariance matrix of the yi​. For the simulation, stipulating s=0.02 changes the conditional uncertainty of a to approximately 0.010892+0.022​=0.02277, despite the same residual pattern. Repeating timings cannot average away this common scale contribution. In the uncorrected continuum model in elementary charge, holding the other measured inputs fixed gives ∣q∣∝η3/2, so a small fractional error in air dynamic viscosity causes 3/2 times that fractional error in inferred electric charge. The gas slip correction to Stokes drag requires its own propagation. Pattern agreement, drop-stability controls and absolute measurement calibration together make the inference persuasive within resolution.

Electrostatic induction

Electric charge OurBigBook.com
Electrostatic induction is redistribution of electric charge in response to an external charged object. An isolated electrical conductor can acquire positive and negative surface regions while its total electric charge stays fixed; see the contact control in electric charge.

Like-charge attraction between conductors

Words: 98 Articles: 1
Electrostatic induction OurBigBook.com
Conductors with net charges of the same sign can attract because their internal charge distributions respond to one another. A point-charge calculation misses this electrostatic induction contribution. Exact conducting-sphere results are given in Electrostatics of Two Charged Conducting Spheres by John Lekner.[ref]

Charged conducting sphere in a slowly varying electric field (U(R)≃kQ1​Q2​/R−kQ12​a3/(2R4))

Words: 65
Like-charge attraction between conductors OurBigBook.com
A small conducting sphere of radius a has electric polarizability α=4πϵ0​a3=a3/k. In the field E≃kQ1​/R2 of a much more strongly charged distant source, its leading induced contribution is −αE2/2, in addition to kQ1​Q2​/R for its fixed net charge. Taking −dU/dR gives FR​≃kQ1​Q2​/R2−2kQ12​a3/R5. The approximation requires a/R≪1 and control of the source's finite-size corrections; the threshold is not an exact finite-sphere result.

Charge neutrality

Words: 102 Articles: 1
Electric charge OurBigBook.com
A system is charge neutral when its total positive and negative electric charge cancel.

Gas-efflux test of charge neutrality

Words: 90
Charge neutrality OurBigBook.com
A sensitive charge neutrality test lets nominally neutral gas escape from an electrically isolated vessel connected to an electrometer. A net charge per escaping molecule would leave a measurable opposite charge on the vessel. Removing stray ions and charged particles is essential. Hydrogen and helium measurements constrain charge imbalance despite different particle binding and internal motions, providing evidence for velocity-independent additive charge rather than a charge proportional to relativistic particle energy. The 1960 experiment used this efflux principle. [ref]

Charge conservation (∂t​ρ+∇⋅J=0)

Words: 514
Electric charge OurBigBook.com
Charge conservation says that the total signed electric charge of an isolated collection stays constant. More generally, a collection closed to electric charge exchange has constant total electric charge, even if energy crosses its boundary. This is the charge bookkeeping relevant to a closed system or an isolated system; isolation from energy exchange is not required. Positive and negative electric charge count with opposite signs. Creating or removing an electron and a Positron together is compatible with charge conservation, because their combined electric charge is zero. [ref].
Imagine a fixed box initially containing electric charge Q(0)=10μC. Stipulate incoming conventional current Iin​=3μA and outgoing conventional current Iout​=1μA throughout 0≤t≤2s, with no other boundary transport. Since one ampere is one coulomb per second, the stored electric charge grows at 2μC/s:
dtdQ​=Iin​−Iout​=2μC/s,Q(t)=10μC+(2μC/s)t,Q(2s)=14μC.
(10)
If instead the outgoing electric current also equals 3μA, the stored electric charge remains 10μC while electric charge passes through. These are stipulated transport examples; constant terminal electric currents alone do not guarantee a time-independent interior charge density.
Locally, charge conservation is the charge continuity equation, an instance of the general continuity equation:
∂t​ρ+∇⋅J=0.
(11)
Here ρ(r,t) is signed volume charge density and J(r,t) is current density. A positive divergence of current density means net outward transport from a small neighborhood, so its charge density decreases. For a fixed control volume V with closed surface ∂V and outward unit normal n, the equivalent integrated balance is
QV​(t)=∫V​ρdV,dtdQV​​=−∮∂V​J⋅ndA=−Iout,net​.
(12)
The surface integral is signed: incoming positive electric charge contributes negatively to outward electric current, and outgoing positive electric charge contributes positively. Integrate the charge continuity equation over fixed V and apply the divergence theorem to obtain this balance. Zero net boundary transport gives constant QV​; the global and local statements describe the same conservation law at different scales. [ref].
In a steady transport state, charge density and current density are time-independent, so the charge continuity equation reduces to ∇⋅J=0. At an electrical circuit junction, choose each terminal electric current Ik​ positive outward and assume the terminals account for all boundary transport. Then
∑k​Ik​=−dtdQjunction​​.
(13)
Kirchhoff's current law, ∑k​Ik​=0, follows when accumulation of electric charge at the junction is negligible. During storage, retain the same balance with its nonzero derivative; charge conservation continues to hold. This makes charge conservation useful for checking electrical circuit models and for tracking the charging of a capacitor. [ref].
The beautiful consistency with Maxwell equations is that the electric field and magnetic field already enforce this transport balance. For sufficiently smooth fields in vacuum SI, take the divergence of the Ampère-Maxwell equation, use that the divergence of a curl is zero, and substitute Gauss's law, ∇⋅E=ρ/ϵ0​. Constant vacuum permittivity ϵ0​ gives
0=∇⋅J+ϵ0​∂t​(∇⋅E)=∇⋅J+∂t​ρ.
(14)

On printed page 36, his relation S=A/L expresses electric current in terms of total driving tension and a reduced length incorporating electrical conductivity and geometry. This is historical notation: his A is not the wire cross-sectional area used here, and his L is not simply the wire's physical length. Drude model
Words: 2k Articles: 8
Electrical conductivity OurBigBook.com
The Drude model explains finite electrical conductivity by balancing charge carrier acceleration in an electric field against loss of directed momentum through collisions. Its useful surprise is that continuous microscopic motion can produce a constant macroscopic current density: the applied electric field continually restores the directed momentum lost to the material. The simplest version has one mobile species, constant number density n, electric charge q, mass m>0, and momentum relaxation time τ>0, in a stationary, homogeneous, isotropic material. At zero magnetic field, its mean drift velocity and current density obey
mdtdvd​​=qE(t)−τmvd​​,J=nqvd​,τdtdJ​+J=σ0​E(t),σ0​=mnq2τ​.
(34)
For electrons, q=−e with positive elementary charge e, so σ0​=ne2τ/m. The electron drift velocity points against a constant electric field, whereas conventional current points along it. Random microscopic velocities can have zero mean without being zero individually; drift velocity is this population mean, rather than each particle's speed.[ref]
The same first-order linear differential equation predicts both Drude current relaxation after switching an electric field and the Drude frequency response to a sinusoidal electric field. Together they let a measured electrical conductivity be interpreted in terms of a density, a mass, and a time scale; a single constant-field measurement determines only their combination nq2τ/m.
The original 1900 paper Zur Elektronentheorie der Metalle by Paul Drude sought a common account of electrical transport and heat transfer using mobile charged particles and ideas from the kinetic theory of gases. Its introduction, especially printed pp. 568–569, explains that comparing different transport phenomena could constrain the populations of free and bound charged particles. The modern momentum relaxation time formulation above is a useful presentation of the model, not a verbatim translation of the original notation or its historical assumptions about mass.[ref]
Momentum relaxation time (τ)
Words: 136
Drude model OurBigBook.com
The momentum relaxation time is the exponential relaxation time of mean directed momentum after the driving electric field is removed. In the simplest Drude model, independent collisions occur with probability dt/τ during a short time interval dt and reset the mean velocity of the collided population to zero. The remaining fraction preserves its previous mean momentum. To first order in dt, averaging gives d⟨p⟩/dt=qE−⟨p⟩/τ. This is a population equation: it does not assert that every particle stops at equally spaced instants.[ref]
For real materials, a collision that changes a particle's direction only slightly need not erase its directed momentum, so the momentum relaxation time need not equal the time between all scattering events. This transport time is also distinct from the bulk charge relaxation time ϵ/σ: one describes loss of directed motion, the other redistribution of charge density.

Starting from zero drift velocity, the current density reaches 1−e−1≈0.632 of its limiting value after one momentum relaxation time. Switching the electric field off at T instead gives J(t)=J(T)e−(t−T)/τ for t≥T. A finite step of electric field changes the acceleration immediately but leaves drift velocity and current density continuous.
More generally, multiplying the current density equation by an integrating factor gives
J(t)=e−(t−t0​)/τJ(t0​)+mnq2​∫t0​t​e−(t−s)/τE(s)ds.
(36)
This is the causal response of a first-order relaxation equation: only earlier electric fields enter the integral. It also shows why instantaneous Ohm's law is an approximation when the electric field changes appreciably during a momentum relaxation time.

(38)
Thus a positive argument of complex conductivity in the e−iωt convention means that current density lags the electric field. At ωτ=1, its real part and imaginary part are both σ0​/2, its modulus is σ0​/2​, and the lag is π/4.
For ωτ≪1, complex conductivity tends to the positive constant σ0​: current density nearly follows the electric field. For ωτ≫1 within this model,

The current density amplitude decreases and its response becomes predominantly inertial. Average power absorbed per volume is p​=21​Reσ∣E∣2≥0. These limits describe the material response to a specified local electric field, not the complete electromagnetic response of a finite specimen with contacts. The Drude response has its pole at ω=−i/τ, consistent with the decaying causal response of a first-order relaxation equation.
The simple Drude model does not predict the microscopic momentum relaxation time. It neglects electronic band structure and Fermi-Dirac statistics; a useful semiclassical extension replaces m by an appropriate band effective mass, but neither a single scalar mass nor one constant momentum relaxation time describes every material. Several charge carriers, energy-dependent scattering, and transitions between electronic bands can spoil the simple Drude frequency response. A successful low-angular frequency fit does not justify extrapolation to arbitrarily large angular frequencies.

Drude conductivity and Hall experiment

Drude model OurBigBook.com
A motivating laboratory realization is The Hall Effect and Conductivity in Germanium by Rex Tayloe. The handout specifies a germanium sample holder with temperature and magnetic field control, a low-voltage supply, digital meters, and a current-reversing switch. Measure the sample dimensions, map the contacts, and establish the directions of electric current, magnetic field, and transverse voltage. At fixed temperature and zero magnetic field, sweep positive and negative electric currents and record longitudinal electric potential differences. A straight voltage-versus-electric current relation tests Ohm's law; sample geometry converts its slope to electrical resistivity. For the Hall effect, minimize the zero-field transverse offset and measure transverse voltage at all four combinations of ±I and ±B, repeating for several electric currents. The readouts test longitudinal proportionality, transverse polarity, and transverse proportionality to electric current. These are protocol instructions, not reported measurement outcomes.[ref]
For interpreting such measurements, an ideal uniform bar of wire cross-sectional area A with longitudinal sensing contacts separated by L gives σ=LI/(AVL​). Four-terminal sensing suppresses voltage drops in current contacts when the voltage meter draws negligible electric current; it does not fix uncertain dimensions or a nonuniform current density. Reverse electric current and use [VL​(+I)−VL​(−I)]/2 to reject a constant voltage offset. Keep temperature stable, allow the current density to settle, and reduce electric current to test for Joule heating. Those are controls for interpreting the material coefficient, rather than reasons to assume every measured curve is linear.
For the transverse measurement define J=Jx​x, B=Bz​z, width w along y, and thickness d along z. Define VH​=V(y=−w/2)−V(y=+w/2)=Ey​w, so Jx​=I/(wd) gives
RH​=Jx​Bz​Ey​​=IBz​dVH​​.
(41)
Extract the part odd in both electric current and magnetic field using
VHodd​=4V(+I,+B)−V(−I,+B)−V(+I,−B)+V(−I,−B)​.
(42)
This combination rejects a constant offset and longitudinal pickup even in magnetic field. It cannot reject another signal with the same two reversal symmetries. Check field polarity and magnitude independently; a sign error in the contact map changes the inferred Hall coefficient.
For one Drude model species in transverse open circuit, the steady Lorentz force balance is 0=q(E+vd​×B)−mvd​/τ with vd,y​=0. Its y component gives Ey​=vd,x​Bz​. Consequently
RH​=nq1​,RH​=−ne1​for electrons,n=e∣RH​∣1​,μ=σ∣RH​∣=meτ​,τ=ne2mσ​.
(43)
Longitudinal electrical conductivity and the Hall coefficient therefore separate number density from charge carrier mobility in this single-species model. Inferring a momentum relaxation time additionally requires an appropriate mass. A constant-field longitudinal measurement alone cannot supply all three.
A Hall coefficient is not universally the reciprocal of signed number density. For example, adding independent electron and electron hole contributions with densities n,p and positive charge carrier mobilities μe​,μh​ in the weak-magnetic field limit gives
σ=e(nμe​+pμh​),RH​=e(nμe​+pμh​)2pμh2​−nμe2​​.
(44)
The Hall coefficient can vanish even while electrical conductivity is positive, and its sign weights charge carrier mobility as well as number density. The germanium handout explicitly asks students to track possible transverse sign changes with temperature; it does not establish a universal single-carrier interpretation. Real electronic band structure and unequal scattering also limit that interpretation.[ref]

Joule heating (P=VI=I2R=V2/R)
Words: 2k Articles: 7
Ohm's law OurBigBook.com
Joule heating is the dissipative conversion of electrical work into internal energy in an electrical conductor. In a metal, the electric field supplies energy to charge carriers, which transfer it to the material. This makes an immersed resistor a useful calibrated heater and makes electrical resistance a source of losses in wiring. Wind-driven electric currents are a proposed source of heating of an inflated giant planet.
For a stationary, purely resistive Ohmic conductor, use the passive sign convention: V is the terminal electric potential difference from the entry to the exit of positive electric current I. The absorbed electrical power and Ohm's law give
P=VI=I2R=RV2​≥0,R>0.
(45)
The last two expressions assume V=IR at the relevant material temperature. For constant electrical resistance and electric current over a duration Δt, the dissipated energy is Ediss​=I2RΔt; otherwise use Ediss​=∫V(t)I(t)dt. In SI, VA=W=J/s.[ref]
Absorbed electrical power VI is more general than Joule heating: a capacitor can store energy, a battery can change its chemical energy, and an electrical circuit can deliver mechanical work or emit light. Even a heated resistor need not show an indefinitely rising temperature: in a thermal steady state, its dissipated power leaves by heat transfer. With the heater inside a calorimeter boundary, electrical input crosses as work; the subsequent heat transfer to the room is a different term in the first law of thermodynamics.

Consider separate ideal resistor experiments with R=5Ω and R=10Ω, each maintained at its specified temperature. The comparison also predicts feedback when a particular resistor's electrical resistance rises with temperature: a supply maintaining electric current increases its heating power, whereas one maintaining terminal electric potential difference reduces it. Predicting the actual temperature still needs the material response R(T) and its heat transfer to the surroundings; a nominal supply setting does not establish which drive is actually constant at the resistor.

An electrical calorimetry experiment asks whether a measured electrical work input accounts for a measured warming. The University of Iowa's demonstration uses an insulated flask containing water, an immersed heater, a thermometer, electrical meters and a timer. Its procedure compares the duration, electrical readings and temperature rise. The following low-power measurement design and synthetic readout develop that idea; they are not measurements reported by the demonstration. [ref]
Use a covered calorimeter with weighed water, an immersed resistor, a calibrated thermometer and gentle stirring. Put an ammeter in series with the heater branch and a high-input-electrical resistance voltmeter across the immersed resistor's terminals. Record V(t), I(t), temperature T(t) and room temperature Ta​(t) before, during and after switching the heater on. Measure the electric potential difference at the heater, rather than at the supply: lead and contact electrical resistance outside the receiving boundary can consume power that never reaches the water. Account for voltmeter loading if the ammeter also includes the sensing branch's electric current.[ref]
The electrical readout gives operating electrical resistance R(t)=V(t)/I(t) when I(t)=0, and power P(t)=V(t)I(t). To test Ohm's law, obtain several pairs at the same temperature; one ratio alone cannot establish a linear response. For small electrical resistance, use four-terminal sensing to exclude lead drops and reverse electric current to test stable offsets from the thermoelectric effect. Use brief low-power resistance measurements if the intended result is the unheated value: the test itself causes Joule heating.
For a covered assembly at approximately constant pressure, with negligible evaporation, negligible endpoint mechanical energy changes and no phase transition, take
Ceff​=mw​cw​+Ccal​,Eel​=∫t0​t1​​VIdt=Ceff​(T1​−T0​)+Qloss,out​−Wstir,on​.
(49)
Here cw​ is the water's specific heat capacity at constant pressure, Ccal​ is the participating vessel, heater and sensor heat capacity, Qloss,out​ is signed outward heat leakage, and Wstir,on​ is stirring work entering the assembly. The storage term approximates its enthalpy change; for a rigid fixed-volume receiver use the corresponding heat capacity at constant volume. Calibrate Ceff​ independently if the purpose is to test electrical input against thermal storage. Using the same heating run to define Ceff​=Eel​/ΔT and then claiming it verifies the equality would be circular.
For the synthetic trace, stipulate V=5V, I=1A, R=5Ω, Ceff​=500J/K, room temperature 20∘C, and loss coefficient G=0.5W/K, with negligible stirring input. The heater runs for 120s, beginning at room temperature. The calorimeter heat-loss correction model is
Ceff​dtdT​=VI−G(T−Ta​),ΔT=GVI​(1−e−GΔt/Ceff​).
(50)
It predicts Eel​=600J, ΔT≈1.13080K, storage 565.398J and outward loss 34.602J. Neglecting leakage undercounts deposited energy by about 5.77%; assuming no loss predicts 1.20K. After switching off, the excess temperature undergoes exponential decay with time constant Ceff​/G=1000s. A cooling slope can estimate G only with known Ceff​ and a credible single-temperature model.
Controls separate causes of a temperature rise. Check the electrical meters' zeros and thermometer calibration; keep water mass, immersion, lid and stirring fixed between runs. Record a heater-off stirred baseline to estimate sensor drift and stirring input. Repeat cooling runs over the same temperature range to estimate environmental heat transfer; a baseline taken only at room temperature cannot measure warming-dependent leakage. Vary electric current while keeping R and initial thermal conditions comparable: corrected deposited energy should scale as I2 for equal durations. An independent calorimeter calibration or known reference heat capacity makes this a quantitative test rather than a qualitative observation.
Finite sensor response, incomplete thermal equilibrium, changing R(T) or heat capacity, evaporation, and imperfect loss corrections limit the inference. A final temperature alone cannot distinguish smaller electrical input from larger heat leakage or a larger participating heat capacity. Agreement tests the stated assembly and its energy accounting; it does not show that all electrical work in arbitrary devices becomes heat.
Historically, the Royal Society's archive description of James Prescott Joule's manuscript dated 13 October 1840 records a coil of wire in a jar of water, a thermometer and a galvanometer, and summarizes his inference that warming depends on electrical resistance and the square of electric current intensity. This electrical experiment precedes Joule's paddle-wheel experiment; the input here is electrical work, whereas the paddle supplies mechanical work. The catalogue, rather than the inaccessible manuscript images, supports this account. [ref]
Watt (W=J/s)
Words: 34
Joule heating OurBigBook.com
The watt is the SI unit of power, one joule per second. Joule heating at 12.5W transfers 125J of energy over a time of 10s if that power stays constant. [ref].
Negative differential resistance (dV/dI<0)
Words: 28
Electrical resistance OurBigBook.com
A local negative slope dV/dI<0 of a current-voltage characteristic, where the inverse slope exists. This differs from negative V/I: a tunnel diode can have positive electric potential difference and positive electric current while dV/dI<0.
